bibliographic.title: Capacity of Generative AI to Interpret Human Emotions From Visual and Textual Data: Pilot Evaluation Study
bibliographic.authors: Zohar Elyoseph; Elad Refoua; Kfir Asraf; Maya Lvovsky; Yoav Shimoni; Dorit Hadar-Shoval
bibliographic.citation_apa: Elyoseph, Z., Refoua, E., Asraf, K., Lvovsky, M., Shimoni, Y., & Hadar-Shoval, D. (2024). Capacity of generative AI to interpret human emotions from visual and textual data: Pilot evaluation study. https://doi.org/10.2196/54369

methodology.study_design: comparative benchmark evaluation using standardized psychological tests
methodology.sample_description: ChatGPT-4 and Google Bard evaluated on Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test and Levels of Emotional Awareness Scale; scores compared to random response patterns and human benchmarks
methodology.technology_context: ChatGPT-4, ChatGPT-3.5, and Google Bard assessed for visual and textual emotion interpretation (mentalizing)

eligibility.exclusion_reason: Empirical pilot study benchmarking LLM emotion-recognition performance; does not address conversational governance, oversight mechanisms, compliance, audit, guardrails, or governance of conversational systems.
eligibility.decision_rationale: The study evaluates ChatGPT-4 and Google Bard on psychological tests of visual and textual mentalizing in mental health contexts. Although it references ethical AI and truncated governance language in conclusions, the central contribution is capability benchmarking, not governance of conversational LLM systems in regulated environments.

appraisal.notes: Pilot evaluation with clearly stated objective and standardized instruments; limited detail on repetitions, prompting protocol, and limitations in provided excerpt.

cerqual.explanation: Methods appear coherent for an emotion-recognition benchmark study, but as a pilot with unclear sample/protocol detail in the provided text, confidence in breadth of findings is limited; relevance to conversational governance in regulated LLM systems is very low.

concepts: Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test

synthesis.main_claim: ChatGPT-4 performs at human benchmark levels on visual emotion interpretation and both ChatGPT and Bard surpass general-population benchmarks on textual emotion interpretation; Bard performs at random levels on the visual task.
synthesis.contribution: Provides empirical pilot evidence comparing specific LLMs on standardized psychological measures of emotional mentalizing in a mental health context.
synthesis.limitations: Pilot design; Bard visual performance near random; governance and ethical implications are only briefly noted at the end of the abstract and are truncated in the provided text.
synthesis.use_in_review: Exclude as central or supporting evidence for conversational governance; may serve only as peripheral background on LLM emotion-recognition capabilities in mental health if needed for context.

evidence.claim: Study objective is benchmarking LLM mentalizing, not conversational governance
evidence.excerpt: The aim of the research was to critically evaluate the capabilities of ChatGPT-4 and Google Bard with regard to their competence in discerning visual mentalizing indicators

evidence.claim: Uses specific LLMs in mental health context
evidence.excerpt: the prominence of large language models in mental health applications, questions persist about their aptitude in emotional comprehension

evidence.claim: Empirical methods use standardized psychological tests
evidence.excerpt: The Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test developed by Baron-Cohen and colleagues was used to assess the models' proficiency in interpreting visual emotional indicators

evidence.claim: ChatGPT-4 outperforms random and aligns with human benchmarks on visual task
evidence.excerpt: ChatGPT-4, displaying a pronounced ability in emotion recognition, secured scores of 26 and 27 in 2 distinct evaluations, significantly deviating from a random response paradigm (P<.001)

evidence.claim: No discernible sex or emotion bias reported for ChatGPT-4
evidence.excerpt: ChatGPT-4 exhibited consistent responses, with no discernible biases pertaining to the sex of the model or the nature of the emotion

evidence.claim: Governance mentioned only peripherally in conclusions
